profiles.meeting_scenario: At a large academic medical center, a clinician-educator and a quality analytics lead are holding a design review of an existing proposal called the "ConnectCare Communication Bundle," which was drafted in response to an internal review showing links between physician-patient communication and better health outcomes. The proposal combines a resident communication workshop, faculty observation during clinic visits, a patient-facing question prompt handout, and a six-week outcome evaluation in ambulatory chronic disease clinics. The agenda is to assess whether the proposal is ready to be sent to the Patient Experience Steering Committee, identify any gaps, and decide what revisions are needed before approval. The expected outcome is apparent agreement on submitting a revised version, even though the two reviewers silently apply different assumptions about readiness, scope, materials, and evaluation procedures.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.expertise: Clinician communication training, residency curriculum design, faculty development
members.background: An internist who leads communication-skills teaching for residents and recently chaired the literature review that informed the ConnectCare proposal.
members.private_state: She wants the steering committee to approve the concept quickly so she can launch a small educational pilot this semester, and she is trying to avoid the proposal being delayed by operational details that she believes can be filled in later.
hidden_assumptions: A proposal is "ready for pilot" if the educational content and general evaluation plan are solid enough for a feasibility launch, even if clinic workflow details are still rough.
The "patient education component" naturally includes supports around the visit such as exam-room prompt cards and take-home sheets, not just materials delivered inside the documented encounter.
When people mention "the communication checklist," they mean the 12-item teaching rubric her team synthesized from the literature review and circulated in the draft.
A six-week follow-up can be done by pulling whatever routine clinical data appear in the chart within that window, and some missing data is acceptable for an early pilot.

members.name: Ravi Shah
members.expertise: Clinic measurement workflows, patient experience reporting, operational rollout planning
members.background: A healthcare operations analyst who supports outpatient quality initiatives and maintains the existing observation and survey infrastructure used across the medical center's clinics.
members.private_state: He wants to prevent the steering committee from approving a pilot that creates untracked clinic work, and he is trying to ensure the proposal can plug into existing operational measurement systems without adding bespoke processes.
hidden_assumptions: A proposal is only "ready for pilot" if clinic managers could execute it next month using defined workflows, named owners, and measurable completion targets.

The "patient education component" refers only to materials that staff deliver during the encounter and can reasonably be tied to visit workflow or documentation, not waiting-room or take-home supports.
When people mention "the communication checklist," they mean the existing 8-item outpatient observation tool already used in audit cycles and data dashboards.

A six-week follow-up implies a fixed patient outreach process, typically a survey or call at roughly six weeks, because cross-clinic chart outcomes are too inconsistent to serve as the operational follow-up method.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the proposal is or will be "ready for pilot."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means ready for a small feasibility launch once the educational package and broad evaluation intent are coherent, with workflow specifics to be refined after steering committee approval.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means ready for an operational pilot only when clinic workflow, ownership, data capture, and local execution details are already specified well enough for immediate implementation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In design reviews, saying something is "ready for pilot" sounds routine and competent; both assume the other is applying the same institutional standard, so neither sees a need to unpack the threshold.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss strengthening the "patient education component."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 includes pre-visit and post-visit supports such as exam-room question prompt cards, posters, and take-home sheets that reinforce communication behaviors around the encounter.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the component is limited to materials directly used during the clinical encounter in ways that fit existing visit workflow and documentation practices.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase feels standard and already settled because both agree patients should be better prepared; the disagreement is only about boundary lines that each sees as obvious and not worth stating.

misalignment_points.topic: Which "communication checklist" they are referring to
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to "the communication checklist" or "the checklist from the review."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the new 12-item faculty coaching rubric synthesized from the literature review and placed in the draft appendix for resident feedback.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the existing 8-item outpatient observation checklist already embedded in his team's audit workflow and dashboard fields.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both tools are plausibly called the communication checklist, both are attached to the proposal materials in some form, and each participant assumes the other is referencing the more institutionally salient version.

misalignment_points.topic: How "six-week follow-up" will actually be executed
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the proposal should include "six-week follow-up" on outcomes.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes six-week follow-up means retrospective chart review of any routine blood pressure, A1c, refill, or follow-up attendance data that happen to appear within six weeks after the index visit.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes six-week follow-up means a structured patient outreach survey or call conducted at about six weeks, because that is the only cross-clinic method he considers operationally comparable.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The timing phrase creates false alignment because it sounds specific enough; both focus on the shared time window and silently fill in the execution method from their own standard practice.

turns.inner_thought: I need this to move forward without getting bogged down in clinic-by-clinic logistics. From my perspective, the proposal is ready for pilot if the workshop, coaching approach, patient-facing pieces, and broad evaluation plan are coherent enough to test feasibility this semester. We can refine workflow details once the steering committee gives us the green light.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time, Ravi. I want to make sure the ConnectCare proposal is ready for pilot before we send it to the Patient Experience Steering Committee. I think we're close, but I'd like to pressure-test the draft and see what absolutely needs tightening first.

turns.inner_thought: The concept is strong, but I need enough operational detail that clinic managers could actually run this next month without inventing new work. I especially want to hear how the patient education component fits into encounter flow, documentation, and ownership, because that's where these pilots usually go off the rails.
turns.utterance: It definitely looks promising. Maybe the best place to start is the patient education component—can you walk me through how you see that working in the ambulatory pilot?

turns.inner_thought: The patient education component is one of the most practical parts: question-prompt cards in exam rooms, a brief handout patients can keep after the visit, and reinforcement around the encounter so patients come in better prepared and leave with reminders. On the clinician side, faculty will coach residents using the 12-item communication checklist from our literature review appendix. That richer rubric is central to the teaching value.
turns.utterance: Sure. The patient education component is meant to give patients a simple structure around the visit, and then faculty reinforce the same communication goals during resident coaching. We also built in use of the communication checklist so the teaching side stays aligned with the rest of the bundle.

turns.inner_thought: Good—if they're using the existing 8-item communication checklist, reporting should plug into our current observation infrastructure without much lift. I still want the patient education component kept close to what staff can reasonably do during the visit, because once it spreads beyond normal workflow, nobody owns it and it becomes invisible in the data.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. If we're using the communication checklist, the reporting piece should be pretty straightforward. And for the patient education component, I think it will land more easily with clinic teams if it stays close to normal visit workflow.

turns.inner_thought: Exactly—the checklist from the review was designed to map onto the communication behaviors the literature actually supports, not just the shorter operational observation items. Faculty need enough granularity to coach residents meaningfully in clinic, and I don't want that diluted just to make the draft look cleaner.
turns.utterance: Right, and the checklist from the review was built specifically to reinforce the communication behaviors that showed up most consistently in the literature, so faculty can give richer feedback during clinic.

turns.inner_thought: I'll let the checklist wording sit for now, but I need to pin down evaluation. Clinic leaders will care less about theory than whether the six-week follow-up creates manual outreach work. If it's a structured follow-up process that can run through existing survey or call pathways, maybe this is manageable; if not, they'll push back hard.
turns.utterance: The other section I think committee members will focus on is evaluation. Clinic leaders are mainly going to want reassurance that the six-week follow-up is lightweight and practical.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, six weeks is enough time to look in the chart for whatever routine indicators show up—follow-up attendance, refill activity, blood pressure, A1c, anything relevant—without building a whole extra apparatus. It's an early pilot, so some missing data is fine as long as we can see directional signal and avoid overengineering.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. At six weeks, we should be able to see whether the communication changes are reflected in patient outcomes without overcomplicating the pilot.

turns.inner_thought: Good, she seems aligned that the six-week follow-up needs to be simple and standardized. If that process is clean and owned, then from an operations standpoint the proposal should be ready for pilot—meaning managers can execute it right away with defined steps and measurable completion targets.
turns.utterance: That sounds fine to me. If the six-week follow-up process is clean, the proposal should be ready for pilot from the committee's perspective.

turns.inner_thought: Great—that sounds like enough support to move this forward. I'll polish the appendices, make sure the communication checklist materials are presented clearly, and send the revised version on. Any clinic-specific workflow details can be finalized after approval once we know which sites want in first.
turns.utterance: Great. Then I'll tighten the appendices, clean up the framing around the checklist, and send the revised draft forward. I think any remaining clinic-specific details can be finalized after approval.

turns.inner_thought: As long as the patient education component is described in a way that feels operationally bounded and the checklist language points clearly to something consistent with our current reporting structure, the steering committee will probably view this as implementation-ready. I'll assume the revision will make that explicit enough.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. Once the patient education component is cleaned up and the checklist language is consistent, I expect a smooth steering committee review.
